planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Gillette is a vigorous common-type fig that tolerates humid, hot summers well, making it a good fit for Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Gillette is a California heirloom common-type fig that sets fruit without pollination, bearing a main crop of medium to large figs with greenish-yellow to bronze skin and sweet, amber-colored flesh in late summer. The tree is notably vigorous and handles sustained summer heat and humidity without the fruit splitting or souring problems that trouble some thinner-skinned varieties. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and prune annually to keep an open framework that makes harvest easier on a tree that can otherwise grow quite large. It is a reliable choice where a dependable single main crop, rather than an early breba crop, is the goal.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Rouge de Bordeaux is a compact, self-fertile French heirloom well suited to containers as well as open-ground planting in warmer zones.

directions: Rouge de Bordeaux, also grown under the synonym Pastiliere, is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region prized for ripening earlier in the season than many common-type figs. The fruit are small to medium with dark purple-black skin and richly flavored, deep red to strawberry-colored flesh. It is self-fertile and sets its crop without caprification, and its moderate, manageable size makes it a good candidate for container growing in regions where winter protection is needed. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and expect an earlier harvest window than later-ripening Bordeaux-region relatives.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; San Pedro is the namesake cultivar of the biferous San Pedro fig type and benefits from a long, hot growing season to ripen its second crop.

directions: San Pedro is the type cultivar of the San Pedro group of biferous figs, which set an early, parthenocarpic breba crop in late spring without any need for pollination. In regions with long, hot summers such as the Gulf Coast it goes on to produce a second, pollinated main crop in late summer, whereas in cooler-summer climates that main crop often fails to ripen. Fruit are medium to large with greenish-yellow to bronze skin and amber to light-pink flesh. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, giving it room to grow into a large tree, and expect its first harvest noticeably earlier in the season than single-crop common-type figs.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
